channel.description: Recent content in nature on Japan Specialty Traveler

item.title: A Hidden Mountain Onsen in Northern Tottori — Guide
item.description: Away from the famous coastal hot springs, the mountains of northern Tottori hide small, secluded onsen for travellers who prefer solitude to resort towns. This hidden bath sits among forested slopes, fed by mineral spring water and framed by the changing seasons — fresh green in early summer, brilliant maples in autumn and snow in winter. There are no crowds, no neon and little in the way of shops, just a quiet, simple soak in a natural mountain setting.

item.title: Akiyoshidai Plateau: Japan's Great Karst Grassland — Guide
item.description: Akiyoshidai is the largest karst plateau in Japan, a vast expanse of rolling green grassland in central Yamaguchi studded with countless jagged white limestone rocks that poke through the turf like grazing sheep. It sits directly above the Akiyoshido cave, the two forming a single geological wonder shaped by rain dissolving limestone over aeons. A scenic road crosses the plateau, walking trails wind among the rocks, and an observation deck takes in the whole sweep of it.

item.title: Akiyoshido Cave: Japan's Largest Limestone Cavern — Guide
item.description: Akiyoshido is the largest limestone cave in Japan and one of the longest in East Asia, carved over hundreds of thousands of years beneath the Akiyoshidai plateau in central Yamaguchi. A well-lit walking route of about a kilometre leads through a cool, cavernous underground world: soaring chambers, an underground river, and remarkable formations including the ‘Hundred Plates’, a hillside of terraced limestone pools, and towering columns and draperies. The cave holds a steady temperature around 17°C year-round, making it refreshing in summer and mild in winter.

item.title: Ariake Mudflats and Mudskippers — Guide
item.description: The Ariake Sea’s enormous tidal flats, exposed for kilometres at low tide, are home to one of Japan’s most endearing creatures: the mudskipper (mutsugoro), an amphibious fish that crawls, hops and skips across the wet mud on its fins, propping itself up and even leaping to defend its territory. Found in few other places in Japan, these comical, bug-eyed fish are a beloved symbol of Saga’s Ariake coast. Along the shore you can watch them and other mudflat life — crabs, shellfish and birds — in their unique tidal habitat, sometimes from viewing spots or on guided walks and tidal-flat experiences.

item.title: Blue Pond (Aoiike) — Guide
item.description: The Blue Pond (Aoiike), near Biei in central Hokkaido, is one of the region’s most famous and photogenic natural wonders — a small pond whose water glows an unearthly, vivid blue. The striking colour is caused by naturally occurring minerals (including aluminium hydroxide) in the water, which scatter light to create the surreal turquoise-blue hue, its exact shade shifting with the light, weather and season. Adding to the otherworldly atmosphere are the bare, silvery trunks of dead larch and birch trees standing eerily in the water, the result of the pond’s formation after erosion-control works in the 1980s.

item.title: Cape Muroto and Tokushima's Wild Pacific Coast — Guide
item.description: South of Tokushima city, the prefecture’s coastline turns wild and elemental as it runs down the Pacific shore toward Cape Muroto, the great cape at the tip of the peninsula that divides Tokushima from Kochi’s Muroto. This is a coast of raw geology and open ocean: sheer rocky headlands, wave-cut platforms of uplifted seabed, crashing surf and vast horizons, quite different from the sheltered Seto Inland Sea in the north. The Muroto area is a UNESCO Global Geopark, its dramatic rock formations telling the story of land rising from the sea.

item.title: Daisekirinzan Karst Park — Guide
item.description: Daisekirinzan, near Cape Hedo at the northern tip of Okinawa’s main island, is a remarkable nature park set on ancient karst terrain thought to be over 200 million years old — one of the world’s northernmost tropical karst landscapes. Formed from uplifted and eroded limestone, the park is a surreal wonderland of towering rock pinnacles, jagged crags, mysterious formations, banyan groves and subtropical forest, all wrapped in a spiritual atmosphere (the area has long been considered sacred).

item.title: Enzan Limestone Cave, Tara — Guide
item.description: Enzan Limestone Cave, in the Tara area of southern Saga, is a small limestone cave offering a cool, quiet underground experience away from the crowds. Formed over long ages as water dissolved the limestone rock, its passages hold stalactites, flowstone and cave formations, lit for visitors to explore on foot. Caves like this stay at a steady cool temperature year-round, making them refreshing on a hot summer day, and offer a glimpse of the slow geological processes shaping the mountains.

item.title: Himure & Akahage Shrines, Bungo-ono — Guide
item.description: In the rural inland region of Bungo-ono in Oita, small local shrines set amid forest, rock and countryside offer a peaceful, authentic experience of rural Shinto worship away from the crowds. Bungo-ono is a landscape shaped by ancient volcanic activity from nearby Mount Aso, giving it dramatic gorges, waterfalls, rock formations and rich soil — a designated UNESCO Global Geopark. Its shrines, often tucked into atmospheric natural settings among old trees, mossy stone and streams, reflect the deep-rooted local connection between the community, the land and its deities.

item.title: Inland Mountain Shrines & Temples — Guide
item.description: Beyond the famous coast and Takachiho, the forested mountains of inland Miyazaki hold atmospheric shrines and temple complexes that offer a quiet, spiritual escape into nature. Set amid ancient cedars, mossy stone steps, streams and mountain scenery, these sacred sites carry a deep sense of age and tranquillity, reflecting the long-rooted local traditions of mountain worship that thread through this region. Weathered wooden halls, torii gates, guardian statues and secluded settings reward visitors who venture inland with a peaceful, contemplative atmosphere that changes beautifully with the seasons — fresh green in spring and summer, brilliant colour in autumn.

item.title: Kamosu Highlands: Quiet Uplands of Central Shimane — Guide
item.description: The Kamosu Highlands are a stretch of gentle upland in central Shimane, a quiet landscape of grassy plateaus, cedar and beech forest and wide open skies that feels a world away from the busy coast. It is a place for slow enjoyment rather than headline attractions: walking trails cross the rolling terrain, wildflowers colour the meadows through the warmer months, and the cool, clear air draws locals for hiking, camping and stargazing.

item.title: Kumamoto Prefectural Museum — Guide
item.description: The Kumamoto Prefectural Museum, near Suizenji Garden, is a broad, family-friendly museum covering the natural history, geology, archaeology and history of Kumamoto prefecture. Its exhibits range across the region’s dynamic natural environment — shaped by the great Aso volcano — its wildlife and fossils, and its human history from ancient times through the samurai era, presented in an accessible, engaging way. A popular highlight is its planetarium, projecting the night sky and astronomy shows, and there are hands-on and interactive displays that make it especially good for children.

item.title: Lake Shikotsu — Guide
item.description: Lake Shikotsu (Shikotsu-ko), within Shikotsu-Toya National Park about an hour south of Sapporo, is a beautiful, deep caldera lake renowned for having some of the clearest, most pristine water in Japan. Formed in a volcanic caldera and ringed by conical peaks including Mount Eniwa and Mount Tarumae, it’s the country’s second-deepest lake and, thanks to its depth, never freezes over even in Hokkaido’s harsh winters. The clear blue water is wonderful for viewing, and visitors can take sightseeing boats or clear-bottomed ‘aqua’ boats, rent canoes and kayaks, or simply enjoy the lakeside scenery and forest walks.

item.title: Mangrove Kayaking on Iriomote — Guide
item.description: Iriomote Island, the largest of the Yaeyama Islands and one of Japan’s last great wildernesses, is around 90% covered in dense subtropical jungle and mangrove forest — earning it the nickname ‘the Galapagos of the East’. Kayaking through its mangrove-lined rivers is the classic way to experience this remarkable natural environment. Guided tours paddle up winding tidal rivers such as the Urauchi and Nakama, gliding quietly between towering mangrove trees whose tangled roots arch over the water, past lush jungle alive with birds, crabs and other wildlife.

item.title: Megami Waterfall — Guide
item.description: Megami Waterfall (Megami-no-taki), in the wooded hills of eastern Nagasaki, is a scenic cascade offering a cool, refreshing escape into nature away from the coast and city. Fed by mountain streams, the falls tumble down mossy rock through a lush green gorge, the water and shade keeping the air pleasantly cool even in summer. A short walk through the forest leads to viewpoints of the cascade, and the surrounding valley is at its most beautiful in the fresh green of late spring and early summer and again when the maples turn in autumn.

item.title: Miyazaki Prefectural Museum — Guide
item.description: The Miyazaki Prefectural Museum of Nature and History, set in the green surroundings of Miyazaki Jingu shrine’s park in the city, is an excellent free introduction to the prefecture. Its wide-ranging exhibits cover Miyazaki’s natural environment — from its subtropical coast to its mountains and wildlife — as well as its rich archaeology and history, including material connected to the ancient burial mounds of Saitobaru and the region’s deep mythological heritage.

item.title: Mount Aso and Nakadake Crater — Guide
item.description: Mount Aso (Aso-san), in the centre of Kumamoto, is one of the world’s most active volcanoes and the beating heart of the region. It sits within one of the largest volcanic calderas on Earth — a vast basin, formed by ancient super-eruptions, that today holds towns, farms and railways ringed by the caldera’s grassy rim. At its centre rise five volcanic peaks, of which Nakadake is still highly active. When conditions allow, visitors can go right up to the rim of Nakadake’s crater and peer down at a steaming, otherworldly turquoise pool of volcanic water, ringed by barren ash-grey slopes and rising fumes — a raw, unforgettable sight found in few other places.

item.title: Mount Daisen: Tottori's Sacred Peak and Trails — Guide
item.description: Mount Daisen is the great peak of western Tottori and the highest mountain in the Chugoku region, a broad volcanic cone that dominates the coastal plain and, seen from the west, echoes the shape of Mount Fuji. It has been a sacred mountain for well over a thousand years, home to Daisen-ji, an ancient mountain temple, and to Ogamiyama Shrine reached by a long stone-paved approach through towering trees. Around it spread Japan’s largest beech forest, walking trails for every level, ski slopes in winter and some of the region’s finest autumn colour.

item.title: Mount Mitake — Guide
item.description: Mount Mitake (Mitake-san), rising about 929 m in the Okutama region of western Tokyo, is a long-revered sacred mountain and a wonderful nature and hiking escape within the metropolis. A cable car whisks visitors up much of the mountain, near the top of which sits a small, atmospheric village of pilgrim lodgings (shukubo) and shops, and the venerable Musashi-Mitake Shrine, reached by a final flight of stone steps and offering fine views.

item.title: Nagai Park & Botanical Garden: Osaka's Southern Green Lung — Guide
item.description: Nagai Park is one of Osaka’s largest green spaces, a broad expanse in the south of the city built around sports stadiums, wide lawns and, at its heart, the Nagai Botanical Garden. The garden lays out themed zones — a large pond, seasonal flower fields, a rose garden and collections of trees — alongside the Osaka Museum of Natural History, whose dinosaur and whale skeletons make the pairing a strong family destination.

item.title: Nagasaki's Outer Islands Day Trip — Guide
item.description: Nagasaki prefecture includes a great many islands scattered across the seas off its long, deeply indented coast, and a day trip out to them offers a relaxed, scenic contrast to the historic city. Reached by ferry or high-speed boat from Nagasaki and other ports, the outlying islands offer clear blue seas, white-sand beaches, rugged coastal scenery, quiet fishing villages and a slower pace of island life. Depending on the island, visitors can swim and snorkel in summer, sample the freshest local seafood, walk coastal paths and viewpoints, and soak up the peaceful, remote atmosphere far from the crowds.

item.title: Naruto Whirlpools: Roaring Tidal Vortexes — Guide
item.description: The Naruto whirlpools are one of Japan’s great natural spectacles, formed where the tides surge through the narrow Naruto Strait between Tokushima and Awaji Island. As enormous volumes of water rush between the Seto Inland Sea and the Pacific with each tide, the clash of currents creates powerful, roaring whirlpools — among the largest in the world, reaching up to 20 metres across at peak spring tides. You can experience them up close from sightseeing boats that nose right to the edge of the swirling water, from above through the glass floor of the Uzu no Michi walkway suspended beneath the Onaruto Bridge, or from viewpoints on shore.

item.title: Ryugado Cave: Kochi's Limestone Wonder — Guide
item.description: Ryugado is counted among Japan’s three great limestone caves, a spectacular cavern carved over a million and a half years into the hills of eastern Kochi. A well-lit walking route of around a kilometre leads through soaring chambers past a wealth of formations — stalactites, flowstone curtains, an underground waterfall and pools — with the added fascination of ancient traces showing that people lived at the cave mouth some two thousand years ago.

item.title: Sekiya Shrine and Its Hidden Waterfall — Guide
item.description: Tucked into the forested hills of western Tottori, Sekiya Shrine and its hidden waterfall are the kind of quiet, off-the-map spot that rewards travellers willing to leave the main sights behind. A modest shrine sits among old trees, its approach cool and green, and a waterfall tumbles nearby, the sound of falling water and birdsong the only company. There are no crowds and no ticket gates — just a peaceful, faintly sacred atmosphere of the sort that once drew mountain ascetics to places like this across the San’in region.

item.title: Shimanto River: Japan's Last Clear Stream — Guide
item.description: The Shimanto is celebrated as ‘the last clear stream in Japan’, a broad, beautiful river that flows for nearly two hundred kilometres through the mountains and countryside of western Kochi without a single large dam on its main course. Its clear green waters, wooded banks and old-fashioned rural scenery make it one of Shikoku’s loveliest landscapes. The river’s signature sight is its chinkabashi — low ‘sinking bridges’ built without railings so that floodwaters pass harmlessly over them, crossing the water in long, simple lines.

item.title: Shofu Lake Scenic Trail near Hagi — Guide
item.description: Away from Hagi’s historic streets, the wooded hills of the interior hold quiet lakes and reservoirs ringed by walking trails, offering a peaceful contrast to the castle town and coast. A scenic lake trail like this one winds along the water’s edge and through the surrounding forest, with still reflections, birdsong and seasonal colour the main rewards — fresh green in spring and early summer, fiery maples in autumn. There are no crowds and no admission, just the simple pleasure of an easy walk in nature.

item.title: Southern Tottori's Gorges and Mountains — Guide
item.description: The southern edge of Tottori, where the prefecture climbs toward the mountains along the Okayama border, is a landscape of forested valleys, clear rivers and quiet gorges quite different from the famous coast. This is deep-country San’in: winding scenic roads, river valleys that blaze with colour in autumn, and hidden temples and shrines set among the peaks — most dramatically Sanbutsu-ji, whose tiny Nageire-do hall clings improbably to a sheer cliff face high on Mount Mitoku, reached only by a demanding pilgrim scramble.

item.title: Takasakiyama Monkey Park — Guide
item.description: Takasakiyama Natural Zoological Garden, on a forested mountain overlooking the sea between Beppu and Oita city, is home to large troops of wild Japanese macaques (snow monkeys) that roam free on the mountain. Numbering well over a thousand across two main troops, the monkeys come down to a feeding area where visitors can watch them at close range as they eat, groom, play and interact, revealing the fascinating social hierarchy and family life of the group.

item.title: Tateba Park and Hiking Trails, Genkai — Guide
item.description: Tateba Park, in the Genkai area of northern Saga, is a natural park offering walking and hiking trails through wooded hills near the coast. Away from the towns and porcelain kilns, it’s a quiet place to stretch your legs in nature: forest paths climb through the trees, opening at points to viewpoints over the surrounding hills and, in places, the Genkai Sea. The trails are pleasant in the fresh green of spring and early summer and glow with colour in autumn, and the park is a favourite for local walkers and families seeking clean air and gentle exercise.

item.title: Tatsuda Shrine — Guide
item.description: Tatsuda Shrine is a serene Shinto shrine in Kumamoto, tucked among woodland and greenery in a quiet setting away from the city bustle. Approached through torii gates and shaded paths, its wooden shrine buildings, mossy stone lanterns and forested grounds create a calm, spiritual atmosphere, especially beautiful in the fresh green of early summer and the coloured leaves of autumn. The Tatsuda area is historically associated with the ruling Hosokawa clan, whose family temple and gardens lie nearby, adding a layer of samurai-era heritage to a visit.

item.title: Todoroki Valley — Guide
item.description: Todoroki Valley (Todoroki Keikoku), in Tokyo’s Setagaya ward, is a remarkable surprise: the city’s only natural ravine, a cool, leafy gorge carved by the Yazawa River that feels a world away from the surrounding suburbs. A pleasant walking path of around 1 km follows the small stream along the valley floor, shaded by dense greenery, crossed by little bridges, and lined with lush ferns and trees, offering a refreshingly cool escape especially in summer.

item.title: Ujitawara Gorge — Guide
item.description: Ujitawara Gorge, in the mountainous Aso region of Kumamoto, is a scenic river gorge offering a cool and refreshing escape into nature. Clear mountain waters flow through a valley of rock formations, pools and greenery, with waterfalls tumbling amid the forest and shaded walking paths following the stream. In the warmer months it’s a wonderfully cooling spot, the water and tree canopy keeping the air fresh even in summer, and in autumn the surrounding maples and foliage turn the gorge into a tapestry of colour.

item.title: Yakushima Island — Guide
item.description: Yakushima, a mountainous island off the southern coast of Kagoshima, is one of Japan’s most extraordinary natural wonders and a UNESCO World Heritage site. Almost circular and covered in dense, ancient forest rising to peaks nearly 2,000 metres high, it is famous above all for its yakusugi — venerable Japanese cedars over 1,000 years old, some far older. The greatest, Jomon Sugi, is thought to be thousands of years old. The island’s misty, moss-carpeted primeval forests are hauntingly beautiful and are said to have inspired the film ‘Princess Mononoke’.

item.title: Kuzuryu River Gorge: A Scenic Ravine Along Fukui's Longest River — Guide
item.description: The Kuzuryu River, named after a mythical nine-headed dragon (kuzuryu) said to have once dwelled in the region, is Fukui’s longest river, and carves a scenic gorge through the inland mountains as it winds toward the coast. The gorge offers a dramatic scenic drive or walk along the water, with steep forested slopes rising on either side, and the autumn foliage season transforms the ravine into one of the region’s most striking seasonal landscapes.

item.title: Shiraito Waterfall: Fukui's 'White Thread' Cascade — Guide
item.description: Shiraito Waterfall takes its name, meaning ‘white thread’, from the way its water spreads and separates into fine, thread-like strands as it cascades down a broad rock face, a gentler and more delicate sight than a single powerful drop of water. Set within a quiet forested valley, the falls are easily accessible via a short walk from nearby parking, making them a good stop for visitors seeking a peaceful natural spot without a demanding hike.

item.title: Shomyo Falls: Japan's Tallest Waterfall — Guide
item.description: Shomyo Falls, at 350 metres, is officially recognised as Japan’s tallest waterfall, dropping in four distinct stages down a sheer volcanic cliff face carved by ancient lava flows near the base of the Tateyama Kurobe Alpine Route. An easy walking trail from the car park leads to a viewing platform facing the falls, and in spring, snowmelt sometimes creates a seasonal fifth-stage cascade known as Hannoki Falls, briefly making the combined drop even more dramatic.

item.title: Arashiyama Guide: Bamboo Grove, Temples & the Hozu River
item.description: On the western edge of Kyoto, where the city meets forested mountains and the Hozu River, lies Arashiyama — a district that packs a soaring bamboo grove, a UNESCO Zen garden, a monkey mountain, riverboats, a scenic railway, and a famous moon-crossing bridge into one beautiful, walkable area. The towering green corridor of the bamboo grove is the headline image, but Arashiyama rewards a full half-day or more of exploring.

item.title: Hokkaido Salmon Fishing Guide: Rivers, Season & Tours
item.description: Salmon are woven into Hokkaido’s culture, cuisine and seasons, and autumn brings one of nature’s great spectacles to the island: the salmon run, when chum and pink salmon surge back from the sea to spawn in the rivers where they were born. For anglers, Hokkaido offers superb shore (surf) and river fishing; for everyone else, watching thousands of salmon battle upstream — or visiting a hatchery and the Sapporo Salmon Museum — is unforgettable.

item.title: Hokkaido Snowshoe Guide: Forest Tours, Season & Tips
item.description: For a peaceful, accessible way to experience Hokkaido’s magical winter, strap on snowshoes and walk out into the silent, snow-laden forest. Snowshoeing lets you float over deep powder that would swallow ordinary boots, following guides into birch woods, frozen wetlands and national-park trails far from the crowds. No experience is needed — if you can walk, you can snowshoe — making it perfect for families and first-time winter adventurers. Look for animal tracks, frost-covered trees and frozen waterfalls, and warm up afterwards in an onsen.

item.title: Kamakura Hiking Guide: Daibutsu Trail, Routes & Access
item.description: Beyond its famous temples and Great Buddha, Kamakura hides a network of leafy hiking trails threading through the forested hills that ring the old samurai capital. The best-known, the Daibutsu Trail, links Kita-Kamakura’s temples to the Great Buddha and Zeniarai Benten shrine, while the longer Tenen Trail traces a ridge with sea views. These easy-to-moderate walks let you escape the crowds, pass tucked-away shrines and bamboo, and stitch the town’s highlights together on foot — a refreshing, scenic way to experience Kamakura that combines nature, history and a workout in a single day.

item.title: Nomizo Falls & Kameiwa Cave Guide: Heart of Light & Access
item.description: Hidden in the forested Kiyosumi Gorge of central Boso, Nomizo Falls and the adjacent Kameiwa Cave are home to one of Chiba’s most magical natural sights. On clear mornings in the right season, sunlight streams through the cave’s tunnel-like opening and reflects off the still water below, forming a luminous, near-perfect heart shape that went viral and now draws photographers from across Japan. Even outside those golden moments, the mossy rock arch, gentle waterfall and emerald stream make a serene, fairy-tale woodland scene.

item.title: Okutama Guide: Tokyo's Wild Mountain Frontier
item.description: Most people are astonished to learn that Tokyo — the word that means glass towers and 37 million people — also contains genuine mountain wilderness. Travel two hours west of Shinjuku and the metropolis gives way entirely to steep forested valleys, crystal-clear rivers, a turquoise reservoir, and limestone caves: this is Okutama, the mountainous far-western edge of Tokyo Prefecture, part of the Chichibu-Tama-Kai National Park. Here you can kayak on a mountain lake, walk through a gorge, descend into a cave, soak in a hot spring, and stand among some of the Kanto region’s finest autumn colour — all without leaving Tokyo.

item.title: Tanzawa Mountains Guide: Hiking, Trails & Access
item.description: Rising in western Kanagawa, the Tanzawa Mountains are one of the most popular hiking ranges within easy reach of Tokyo — a green wall of ridges, valleys and waterfalls protected as a quasi-national park. Well-marked trails, mountain huts and ridgeline views (including Mt. Fuji on clear days) draw weekend hikers in every season, from spring greenery and summer escapes from the heat to fiery autumn colours. The signature climb is Mt.

item.title: Tokachi Millennium Forest Guide: Gardens, Tickets & Access
item.description: In the rolling countryside of the Tokachi plain lies the Tokachi Millennium Forest, one of Japan’s most celebrated contemporary gardens. Conceived as a 1,000-year project to reconnect people with nature, it blends manicured garden artistry with the wild Hokkaido landscape — most famously the sculpted, wave-like grass mounds of the Earth Garden and the lush perennial borders of the Meadow Garden, designed by acclaimed plantsman Piet Oudolf. An international garden-design award-winner, it’s a serene, beautiful stop, with goats, cafés, cycling and forest trails to enjoy at a gentle pace.

item.title: Yanbaru Guide: UNESCO Forest, Wildlife & Access
item.description: The lush, mountainous north of Okinawa Island is Yanbaru — a subtropical forest so biodiverse it was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage natural site in 2021. Home to rare endemic creatures found nowhere else on Earth, like the flightless Okinawa rail (Yanbaru kuina) and the Okinawa woodpecker, it offers a completely different Okinawa from the beaches: dense green ridges, waterfalls, mangroves and the dramatic karst formations of Daisekirinzan. It’s the island’s premier destination for nature lovers.

item.title: Yoro Valley Guide: Onsen, Autumn Leaves & Access
item.description: Tucked into the green heart of the Boso Peninsula, Yoro Valley (Yorokeikoku) is Chiba’s premier nature escape — a winding river gorge of clear pools, waterfalls and forested ridges that erupts into brilliant colour each autumn. It’s one of the latest-colouring autumn-leaf spots near Tokyo (late November to early December), and its riverside onsen ryokan let you soak among the foliage. Walking trails lead to the photogenic Awamata Falls and a curious old road tunnel, while the rural Kominato and Isumi railways make getting there half the fun.

item.title: Hiroshima Nature Guide: Miyajima, Shimanami Kaido & Taishakukyo Gorge
item.description: Most visitors arrive in Hiroshima expecting a city, and leave surprised by the breadth of its natural landscape. The prefecture stretches from the islands of the Seto Inland Sea up to the mountainous border with Shimane, and along the way passes a sacred forest mountain, two world-class gorges, an island-hopping cycling route considered among the best in Asia, and dozens of small islands with their own micro-cultures of citrus, fishing, and slow time.

item.title: Wakayama Nature: Kumano Kodo Trails, Nachi Falls & Sea Turtle Beaches
item.description: The Kii Peninsula, which makes up most of Wakayama Prefecture, contains some of the most biologically and geologically diverse terrain in Japan. Warm, rain-drenched mountains rise abruptly from a Pacific coastline shaped by the Kuroshio Current — Japan’s equivalent of the Gulf Stream — moderating the climate just enough to support subtropical species more than 300 kilometres north of their usual range. The result is a landscape where ancient cedar forests meet coral reefs, where Japan’s tallest waterfall drops into UNESCO-listed primeval forest, and where sea turtles nest on beaches that also see summer holidaymakers from Osaka.

item.title: Kamikochi: Complete Guide to Japan's Most Beautiful Alpine Valley
item.description: Kamikochi is a 15-kilometre alpine basin in the Northern Japan Alps, carved by the Azusa River and enclosed by peaks that include the 3,190-metre Okuhot-akadake. At 1,500 metres above sea level, it is one of the highest and most spectacular valleys accessible to ordinary visitors anywhere in Japan — yet it requires no hiking, no special equipment, and no particular fitness. A bus from Matsumoto stops at the valley floor, where flat paths follow the river through ancient larch forest past mirror-still ponds and beneath rock faces that rise several hundred metres above the trees.

item.title: Aomori Nature: Oirase Stream, Shirakami-Sanchi Beech Forest & Osorezan
item.description: Aomori Prefecture Nature and Outdoor Guide Occupying the northernmost tip of Honshu, Aomori Prefecture offers some of Japan’s most pristine wilderness experiences. From UNESCO World Heritage beech forests to volcanic sacred mountains, this comprehensive guide covers the prefecture’s essential natural wonders for international visitors seeking authentic outdoor encounters. 1. Oirase Stream (奥入瀬渓流) Overview This 14-kilometer gorge, designated a National Scenic Treasure, flows through primeval forest from Lake Towada toward Yakeyama. The Oirase Stream represents one of Japan’s most photographed natural landscapes, where crystalline water cascades over moss-covered volcanic rocks beneath a canopy of ancient trees.

item.title: Fukushima Nature: Bandai Volcanic Highland, Goshiki-numa Lakes & Flower Country
item.description: Fukushima Prefecture Nature & Outdoor Guide Fukushima Prefecture, stretching from the Pacific coast to the central mountains of Honshu, offers some of Japan’s most dramatic volcanic landscapes, pristine forests, and accessible highland trails. Despite lingering misconceptions, the prefecture’s natural areas are safe, spectacular, and surprisingly uncrowded—making them ideal for international visitors seeking authentic Japanese nature experiences away from the tourist crowds. 1. Bandai-Asahi National Park & Mount Bandai (磐梯朝日国立公園・磐梯山) The catastrophic eruption of Mount Bandai in 1888 transformed the landscape forever, creating over 300 lakes and ponds across what is now known as the Urabandai (Back-Bandai) highland.

item.title: Iwate Nature: Sanriku Coast, Iwate-san Volcano & Hayachine Mountain
item.description: Iwate Prefecture Nature & Outdoor Guide for International Visitors Stretching from the Pacific coast to mountainous interior highlands, Iwate Prefecture offers some of northern Japan’s most spectacular and unspoiled natural landscapes. This guide covers essential outdoor destinations, from dramatic coastal cliffs to sacred peaks and ancient limestone caves. 1. Sanriku Fukko National Park: Where Mountains Meet the Sea The Landscape The Sanriku coast is Japan’s premier example of ria coastline—a drowned river valley landscape where ancient mountains have been partially submerged, creating a complex shoreline of deep inlets, rugged headlands, and isolated coves.

item.title: Miyagi Nature: Naruko Gorge Autumn Leaves, Sanriku Coast & Tohoku Wilderness
item.description: Miyagi Prefecture Nature and Outdoor Guide for International Visitors Miyagi Prefecture, anchored by the modern city of Sendai in Japan’s Tohoku region, offers extraordinary natural diversity—from one of Japan’s most celebrated gorges to a rugged Pacific coastline shaped by both geological forces and recent history. This guide reveals the prefecture’s finest outdoor experiences for international visitors seeking authentic encounters with Japanese nature and meaningful cultural landscapes. 1. Naruko Gorge (鳴子峡): Tohoku’s Autumn Masterpiece Naruko Gorge ranks among Japan’s most spectacular autumn destinations, though it remains refreshingly uncrowded compared to Kyoto’s famous sites.

item.title: Niigata Nature: Snow Country Mountains, Sado Island Wilderness & Rice Paddy Landscapes
item.description: Niigata Prefecture Nature & Outdoor Guide Niigata Prefecture stretches along the Sea of Japan coast, blessed with extraordinary natural diversity—from Japan’s deepest snowfalls to endless rice paddies, volcanic mountains to wild Pacific cliffs. This comprehensive guide introduces international visitors to Niigata’s most compelling outdoor experiences. 1. Snow Country Mountain Scenery The World’s Heaviest Snowfalls The Uonuma and Yuzawa highlands, immortalized in Yasunari Kawabata’s novel Snow Country, receive 8–12 metres of snow annually—among the heaviest snowfalls of any inhabited place on earth.

item.title: Toyama Nature Guide: Tateyama Snow Corridor, Shomyo Falls & Gokayama's Deep Valley
item.description: Toyama Prefecture occupies one of the most extreme vertical landscapes in Japan. Within a horizontal distance of roughly 70 kilometres, the terrain drops from 3,000-metre alpine peaks to a bay that plunges 1,000 metres below sea level. This compression produces natural spectacles at every altitude: volcanic crater lakes, walls of snow taller than buildings, Japan’s highest single-drop waterfall, and a coastal sea that lights up blue at night. The Tateyama Mountain Chain The Tateyama range forms the spine of Toyama’s eastern border.

item.title: Yamagata Nature: Dewa Sanzan Sacred Mountains, Zao Crater Lake & Mogami Gorge
item.description: Yamagata Prefecture Nature and Outdoor Guide Yamagata Prefecture, nestled in the Tohoku region of northern Honshu, offers international visitors an extraordinary blend of spiritual mountain pilgrimage, volcanic landscapes, and agricultural beauty that remains largely undiscovered by overseas travelers. From sacred peaks where ancient ascetics trained to snow monsters frozen in Siberian winds, Yamagata delivers some of Japan’s most distinctive outdoor experiences. Dewa Sanzan: The Three Sacred Mountains The Dewa Sanzan—Mt Haguro, Mt Gassan, and Mt Yudono—form the spiritual heart of Yamagata and represent birth, death, and rebirth in the Shugendo mountain religion.

item.title: Fukui Nature: Tojinbo Cliffs, Echizen Coast & Mountain Valleys
item.description: Fukui Prefecture sits along Japan’s Sea of Japan coast, a region long overshadowed by the Shinkansen corridors connecting Tokyo, Kyoto, and Osaka. That relative obscurity has proven to be its greatest gift. The coastline here is raw and elemental — black volcanic cliffs dropping into churning grey-green surf, fishing villages wedged between rocky headlands, and shoreline roads where you can drive for thirty minutes without passing another tourist. Inland, ancient cedar forests shelter Zen temples where silence is practiced as a discipline, and interconnected lakes shimmer in colors that shift with the depth and salinity of the water.

item.title: Hyogo Nature: Mt. Rokko, Awaji Island & Coastal Trails
item.description: Hyogo Prefecture stretches across one of Japan’s most geographically diverse corridors, running from the Pacific-facing shores of the Seto Inland Sea all the way north to the dramatic cliffs and hidden beaches of the Sea of Japan coast. Between these two edges lies an interior of forested mountains, river valleys, and historic castle towns. Few Japanese prefectures can offer a visitor alpine wildflower meadows, oceanic tidal whirlpools, fishing village seascapes, and terraced rural farmland within a single day’s travel.

item.title: Shimane Nature Guide: Oki Islands UNESCO Geopark & Dramatic Coastlines
item.description: Shimane’s most dramatic nature lies offshore. The Oki Islands sit 60 kilometers out in the Sea of Japan — remote enough that ancient Japan used them as an island of exile for deposed emperors and unwanted nobles. Today the islands are a UNESCO Global Geopark, recognized for geological formations that tell 600 million years of tectonic history. On the mainland, the Shimane Peninsula’s rocky Sea of Japan coast and the inland Sanbe volcanic highlands round out a nature itinerary that rewards travelers willing to move beyond the main shrine circuit.

item.title: Tottori Nature Guide: Uradome Coast, Mount Daisen & Seasonal Landscapes
item.description: Tottori’s natural variety is compressed into a narrow geography: a coastline of dunes, sea cliffs, and beaches, then an immediate rise to 1,700m mountain peaks. The San’in coast is one of Japan’s most geologically active stretches of shoreline; the inland mountains carry some of the country’s finest beech forest. The prefecture’s low population density means these landscapes see a fraction of the visitors that equivalent sites in Kyushu or Chubu would attract.

item.title: Chiba Nature Guide: Kujukuri Beach, Boso Peninsula & Coastal Landscapes
item.description: Chiba Prefecture is the closest coastal wilderness to Tokyo — a long peninsula curling into the Pacific with 66 kilometres of unbroken sandy beach on one side, dramatic cliffs and fishing villages on the other, and a forested interior largely unknown to foreign visitors. Its natural landscapes shift with the seasons in ways that reward return visits: winter flower fields, spring rapeseed and cherry blossoms along a country railway line, summer surf beaches, and autumn foliage in the gorge country of the central hills.

item.title: Yamanashi Nature Guide: Climbing Mt Fuji, Shosenkyo Gorge & the Southern Alps
item.description: Yamanashi is defined by extremes of elevation. The prefecture sits in the Kofu Basin at around 250 metres above sea level, but its borders encompass the summit of Japan — Mt Fuji at 3,776 metres — and the highest peaks of the Southern Alps to the west, including Mt Kitadake at 3,193 metres, the country’s second-tallest mountain. Between these extremes stretches a terrain of granite gorges, lava field forests, volcanic ice caves, and river valleys that together constitute one of Japan’s richest and most varied natural environments.

item.title: Nara Nature: Yoshino Cherry Blossoms, Kasugayama Forest & Sacred Landscapes
item.description: Nara Prefecture extends far south of its compact historic city into the vast Kii Peninsula mountain range — one of Japan’s largest areas of wilderness, designated UNESCO World Heritage for its sacred mountain landscapes and ancient pilgrimage routes. The prefecture’s natural world ranges from a 1,300-year-old urban forest that has never been logged to a 30,000-tree cherry blossom landscape that has been celebrated in Japanese poetry since the 8th century. For nature travellers, the southern two-thirds of Nara Prefecture — largely unknown outside Japan — is extraordinary.

item.title: Gunma Nature: Oze National Park, Mt. Akagi & Lake Haruna
item.description: Gunma’s mountains cover the greater part of the prefecture, rising from the flat Kanto plain in the south to volcanic ridges and alpine wetlands along the northern border with Niigata and Fukushima. The variety of terrain is wide — ancient shield volcanoes with caldera lakes, narrow river gorges cut by glacial meltwater, and elevated marshes that exist only because the altitude keeps them frozen for half the year. For outdoor travelers, Gunma is one of the most rewarding prefectures within two hours of Tokyo.

item.title: Ibaraki Nature: Hitachi Seaside Park, Lake Kasumigaura & Mt. Tsukuba
item.description: Ibaraki is not a mountainous prefecture. It has no dramatic alpine passes, no volcanic peaks trailing smoke. What it has instead is a wide, level landscape meeting the Pacific Ocean, a lake that stretches to the horizon, a lone mountain rising above the Kanto Plain, and a coastal park that turns entirely blue for two weeks each spring. The scale of Ibaraki’s natural features is horizontal and panoramic rather than vertical — which makes it one of the most rewarding prefectures in Japan for cycling, walking, and the kind of slow outdoor travel that produces genuinely memorable views.

item.title: Iya Valley, Tokushima: Vine Bridges, Gorges, and Japan's Most Remote Landscape
item.description: The Iya Valley is the kind of place that takes most visitors by surprise. Japan, in the popular imagination, is a country of shinkansen corridors, urban density, and crowded tourist circuits. The Iya Valley is none of these things. Carved over millennia by the Iya River through the mountains of central Shikoku, it is a landscape of near-vertical gorge walls, vine bridges strung between cliff faces, and village communities so isolated that feudal-era fugitives — the defeated Heike clan after the twelfth-century Genpei War — chose these mountains as their final refuge precisely because no army could follow them in.

item.title: Kerama Islands & Okinawa Coral Reefs: The Complete Guide
item.description: The Kerama Islands — 30 km west of Naha — contain some of the most pristine coral reefs in East Asia. Marine biologists have recorded over 250 species of coral and 360 species of fish in the Kerama Shoto National Park. The water clarity here — what the Japanese call “Kerama Blue” (ケラマブルー) — is the result of both the Kuroshio Current and the absence of agricultural runoff on these small uninhabited or lightly populated islands.

item.title: Lake Biwa Complete Guide: Japan's Ancient Inland Sea
item.description: Lake Biwa is not simply a large lake. At 670 square kilometres, it is Japan’s largest body of freshwater, and its shores have been inhabited, crossed, worshipped, and fought over for at least fourteen centuries. The lake predates the oldest surviving structures on its banks; its name derives from the biwa lute, whose shape the water body loosely resembles when viewed from the surrounding mountains. For overseas visitors who know Shiga at all, they tend to know it as the prefecture that contains Lake Biwa — and they are right to think of the lake first, because everything in Shiga orbits around it.

item.title: Nikko Nature: Kegon Falls, Lake Chuzenji & Okunikko
item.description: Tochigi’s natural landscape is dominated by the mountains and waterways of Nikko National Park. Within a 30-kilometre arc north of Nikko town, the terrain rises from cedar forest through alpine lake shoreline to open highland marshland and active volcanic ridges. The concentration of natural features — waterfalls, caldera lake, wetland plateau, gorge — within a single day-trip area from Tokyo is unusual even by Japanese standards. This guide covers the main natural destinations in order of access from Nikko town, with practical details on transport, access costs, and the best times to visit each.

item.title: Saitama Nature: Shibazakura, Chichibu Mountains & Nagatoro Gorge
item.description: Saitama Prefecture stretches from the flat agricultural plains immediately north of Tokyo all the way into the Chichibu mountain range along its western edge. This geographic range — from gentle river valleys and lotus wetlands in the east to dense cedar forests and alpine ridgelines in the west — gives the prefecture a seasonal variety that surprises most visitors who think of it primarily as suburban Tokyo. The Arakawa River cuts through dramatic rock gorges.

item.title: Shimanto River Guide: Canoeing, Cycling, and Japan's Last Wild River
item.description: The Shimanto River flows 194 kilometres from its source in the Shikoku Mountains to the Pacific Ocean at Nakamura City — and it does so without passing through a single dam. It is the only major river in Japan that has never been obstructed along its entire length, a fact that has preserved an aquatic ecosystem of unusual richness and given the river a visual clarity that larger managed rivers have long since lost.

item.title: Hokkaido Nature Guide: Shiretoko, Daisetsuzan, Furano & Kushiro
item.description: Hokkaido’s nature operates on a scale that Japan’s other islands cannot match. The island is 83,000 square kilometres — roughly the size of Austria — and contains 6 national parks, including Japan’s largest (Daisetsuzan) and one of its two UNESCO World Heritage natural sites (Shiretoko). The wildlife is genuinely wild: brown bears that fish for salmon in rivers accessible from the road, red-crowned cranes that are among the world’s rarest birds, and an autumn foliage season that begins 3–4 weeks before the rest of Japan.

item.title: Osaka Nature: Minoo Falls, Castle Park, Osaka Bay & Hidden Green Spaces
item.description: Osaka’s nature reputation — largely non-existent in most travel writing — significantly undersells the city’s green spaces. Within 40 minutes of Namba, you can reach a mountain waterfall surrounded by ancient maple forest; within 20 minutes of Umeda, you can walk a 4km canal path lined with 5,000 cherry trees. The city’s parks are consistently underused by tourists, which makes them among the best nature experiences available in Japan: the quality is high, the crowds are minimal.

item.title: Kanagawa Nature Guide: Hakone Volcanoes, Kamakura Trails & Shonan Coast
item.description: Kanagawa contains more ecological variety than any other prefecture near Tokyo. Within 90 minutes of Shinjuku you can stand inside an active volcanic crater, hike a mountain ridge used by samurai armies, surf a Pacific beach, or kayak among sea caves on a wild volcanic cape. The prefecture is almost entirely overlooked by nature travellers who default to the Japanese Alps — a significant mistake. item.title: Kyoto Nature: Bamboo Groves, Mountain Hikes & Seasonal Gardens
item.description: Kyoto’s nature is inseparable from its culture — the city’s temples and shrines were built to frame specific views of mountains, rivers, and seasonal trees. Cherry blossoms at the Philosopher’s Path, autumn maples at Jojakko-ji, moss gardens at Saihoji, cedar forest at Fushimi Inari — each experience is both natural and profoundly designed. This guide covers Kyoto’s finest nature experiences, with the practical timing that makes the difference between the experience and a photograph of the experience.

item.title: Tokyo Nature Escapes: Parks & Mountains
item.description: Despite being the world’s largest metropolis, Tokyo is surrounded by mountains, threaded with rivers, and punctuated by remarkable gardens — some of them former samurai estates, others primeval forest that has never been felled. This guide covers the best green spaces within the city and the finest mountain escapes within a two-hour train journey. In the City: Parks & Gardens 新宿御苑 — Shinjuku Gyoen National Garden Access: Shinjuku-Gyoenmae Station (Tokyo Metro Marunouchi Line) — 5 min walk Hours: 9:00–16:30 (closed Monday; open daily during cherry blossom season) Entry: ¥500

item.title: Noto Peninsula Road Trip Guide: Senmaida, Wajima & the Sea of Japan Coast
item.description: The Noto Peninsula extends northward from Kanazawa into the Sea of Japan like a finger pointing toward the Korean coast — a narrow strip of land, roughly 60 kilometres from base to tip, whose distance from any large city has preserved a way of life that has disappeared from most of rural Japan. Here, fishing communities still operate according to seasonal rhythms set centuries ago. Traditional farm families maintain the terraced rice paddies that cascade down hillsides to the sea.
